questions.question: How do you reverse a string in Go?
questions.title: Reverse String Go
questions.direct_answer: []rune(s) + swap ends inward — rune-safe. Byte reversal corrupts multibyte UTF-8 (é's two bytes reversed = garbage). Verified: "hello" → "olleh".

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[héllo] -->|[]rune| R[104 233 108 108 111]
    R -->|swap ends| R2[111 108 108 233 104]
    R2 -->|string| O[olléh]
    B[héllo] →|[]byte| BY[104 195 169 108 108 111]
    BY →|swap| BY2[111 108 108 169 195 104]
    BY2 → X[invalid UTF-8]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The grapheme caveat for the perfect answer: rune reversal reverses code points, not graphemes — "é" as e + combining-accent (two runes) stays reversed as accent + e (the accent attaches to the wrong character). True grapheme-safe reversal needs a segmenter (x/text or uniseg). For interviews, rune-reversal with the grapheme caveat is the complete answer.

The allocation-free alternative for hot paths: walk both ends simultaneously with utf8.DecodeRuneInString (forward) and utf8.DecodeLastRuneInString (backward) — swapping into a pre-allocated []byte. Zero rune-slice allocation. The readable []rune version is the default; the optimized version only when profiling demands.

The interview short-circuit: this question is really 'do you know strings are bytes + runes exist?' — the candidate who reaches for []byte(s) without mentioning the trap, or reverses bytes without knowing the corruption, reveals the gap.
